title: The Cost of Capacity Is the Real Story of Trucking’s Most Unusual Year Since Deregulation in 1981
summary: Explore how carrier capacity costs influence freight rates, broker margins, and transportation market trends in trucking.
body_markdown:
Forty-five years after deregulation, the U.S. truckload market is defying its familiar cycle. Although the COVID-era trucking cycle was arguably the most unusual, its extreme swings still followed a familiar pattern: a surge in demand followed by a two-year recovery.


2026 is different. Key themes emerging from recent earnings reports from major domestic trucking firms indicate that spot rates and tender rejections are elevated, yet freight volumes remain soft to flat. Shippers are paying more, but operations are also costing more. This translates to a weak boom defined not by consumer strength, but by highly inflated rates with simultaneous increases in cost where operating leverage joins the litany of other well documented risks in this cycle.


*[Triumph Freight Intelligence Indices](https://triumph.io/solutions/triumph-market-insights/)*


Scarcity of capacity which typically drives rate increases is only part of the explanation. Escalating operating costs are pushing rates higher while eroding carrier margins. In a typical recovery, rates rise against relatively stable costs, expanding profits and encouraging investment. This time, higher expenses are absorbing the gains and likely delaying expansion. Shippers are paying more, but carriers are not necessarily earning enough to expand or modernize their fleets. Based on remarks during many Q3 earnings reports from public tricking firms, the price signal that normally attracts supply appears to be delivering a weaker response which will likely prolong the cycle.


### **What the Cost Stack Looks Like Right Now**


Operating costs extend beyond fuel and driver pay. Equipment, financing, insurance, maintenance, and lost productivity all increase the revenue needed to keep a truck running. Rate gains must be measured against these costs.


Key pieces of the stack in the current environment:


- **Fuel:** Record high diesel prices, which are up[$1.234 y/y as of 10/26/2026 according to eia.gov](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/) , create both an expense problem and a working-capital threat, especially for small fleets and owner-operators. Fuel must be purchased before freight payments and surcharges arrive. More cash becomes tied up in each load, leaving less for payroll, insurance, maintenance, and debt service. Even eventual cost recovery does not eliminate the liquidity gap: a load can cover its costs on paper while leaving the carrier short of cash to fund the next trip. Until payment arrives, the operator must finance successive fuel purchases from cash reserves or available credit. As diesel prices rise, the same cash balance supports fewer trips, potentially forcing a carrier to limit operations even when freight is available and rates cover the expense.


- **Drivers:** Compensation remains a major expense, but availability and compliance increasingly constrain productive capacity. Drug and alcohol restrictions, English-language proficiency enforcement, non-domiciled CDL requirements, and training scrutiny are limiting the available pool to seat trucks.[FMCSA has reported nearly 10,000 CDL schools](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/fmcsa-removes-10000-plus-driver-training-providers-amid-safety-push) have been removed as a result of unsafe practices creating additional bottlenecks for the inflow of new drivers.


- **Equipment and risk:** Financing costs, uncertain equipment values, insurance inflation, and repairs increase the capital required to operate and the return needed to justify investment.


- **Productivity:** Empty miles, dwell, and compliance friction spread expenses across fewer revenue-producing miles. The effective cost per loaded mile can rise even when individual inputs stabilize. Lost productivity and fuel are also interwoven; deadhead and empty miles are just added fuel expense adding more to the pain of lost productivity.


An unseated tractor is not readily available capacity. Returning it to service requires a qualified driver, insurance, working capital, and freight that supports the full operating cost.


### **Why Supply Is Not Responding the Way It Used To**


Normally, rising rates attract new entrants and encourage existing fleets to expand. That adjustment is slower when higher revenue does not produce materially better margins and entry requires more capital.


Authority registrations alone are an incomplete measure of supply. A registration does not guarantee an insured carrier, a seated tractor, or productive miles. Likewise, equipment orders can reflect replacement and purchasing ahead of emissions requirements rather than net fleet growth.


According to many[recent earnings reports](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/category/news/business/finance/company-earnings) , larger fleets are emphasizing yield and utilization over expansion. Smaller operators face tighter financing and liquidity constraints. Across both groups, finding compliant drivers and covering the full cost of operation can matter more than buying another truck. Capacity can therefore continue leaving even as rates rise.


### **Demand Is Not the Driver**


Freight demand is providing support, not a broad surge. When capacity contracts faster than freight demand, pricing can strengthen despite flat or declining volumes. Elevated rejections and route-guide failures reflect that imbalance. Seasonal peaks then hit a network with less slack.


Shippers can substitute intermodal, private fleets, other services, or delayed shipments where practical. Those options are limited for time-sensitive freight, and redesigning networks takes time. Soft demand alone does not ensure soft rates when usable supply is shrinking.


Using proprietary data from the[Triumph Intelligence](https://triumph.io/solutions/triumph-market-insights/) platform, the same-store analysis across hundreds of broker networks below tracks volumes by equipment type, indexed as a percent change to January 2026. Trends are mixed: data-center-driven flatbed growth is slowing, refrigerated volumes are down year to date, and dry van volumes have eased slightly from midyear highs.

### **What This Means for Rates and the Path Ahead**


The outlook depends on whether rates can rise faster than costs, restoring carrier margins enough to fund new capacity. Higher all-in prices alone do not signal a durable recovery, especially when fuel and broader inflation absorb part of each increase. Bid timing adds a lag: larger, more disciplined shippers reset contract rates only at scheduled bids, so their pricing trails current market conditions. When costs will stabilize, and how much of any margin improvement will become new productive capacity, remain uncertain.


Demand adds another uncertainty. Further weakness could ease capacity pressure, while seasonal peaks could strain a network with little slack. Equipment orders and authority registrations will not, by themselves, resolve the supply question: additional trucks must be seated, insured, financed, and profitably deployed. Until those conditions improve, higher rates may coexist with weak carrier economics and a limited supply response.


For shippers entering bidding season, the challenge is to distinguish temporary price pressure from a lasting increase in the cost of reliable capacity. Contract strategies must account for both the risk of continued tightness and the possibility that weaker demand relieves it. Triumph will continue tracking volumes, costs, payment conditions, and capacity signals across its audit, factoring, payments, and intelligence platforms to assess how these uncertainties unfold.
